keyVerseText: And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew adjective עֶלְיוֹן (ʻelyôwn) derives from the root עָלָה (ʻâlâh), which means 'to rise up' or 'to ascend.' This etymology highlights the idea of elevation or going upward, which enriches the common English gloss of 'most high' by emphasizing the concept of being lifted above or exalted. Rather than simply indicating height, the root conveys active movement or elevation, suggesting superiority and exaltation in status or position.
usageInScripture: The word עֶלְיוֹן appears 53 times in the Hebrew Bible and is translated variously as 'of the most High,' 'the upper,' 'most high,' and 'the most high,' among others. These translations reveal a consistent theme of supreme elevation, whether referring to God as the 'Most High' or to earthly rulers exalted above others. The term can function as an adjective describing something physically or metaphorically elevated, as well as a noun used as a title for God or exalted beings, underscoring its flexible yet consistently lofty sense.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עֶלְיוֹן as rooted in the concept of rising or ascending deepens our grasp of God's nature as supremely exalted above all creation. This word conveys not just God's height but His unrivaled sovereignty and authority over all rulers and powers. It reminds believers that God is the ultimate High King, above any earthly monarch or angelic prince, affirming His supremacy and the security of those who trust in Him. Recognizing God as עֶלְיוֹן encourages worship and trust in His exalted position, which is foundational for Christian faith and devotion.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 14:18 introduces Melchizedek as 'the priest of the most high God,' using עֶלְיוֹן to identify God as supremely exalted. This phrase highlights God's unmatched sovereignty and sets the tone for Melchizedek's priestly role as one connected to the highest divine authority. The word עֶלְיוֹן here underscores that Melchizedek's priesthood is not linked to any earthly power but to the transcendent Most High, inviting believers to acknowledge God's supreme lordship in both worship and life.
